source.title_on_document: The Homogenizing Effect of Large Language Models on Human Expression and Thought

paper_design_summary: A narrative review (opinion-style synthesis) that discusses evidence from linguistics, psychology, cognitive science, and computer science on how LLMs homogenize language, perspective, and reasoning. It reports no new data, no systematic search, and no pooled estimates. Its only creativity-specific passage summarizes two cited experiments on LLM-assisted ideation (refs. 124 and 125: Anderson, Shah, and Kreminski 2024; Doshi and Hauser 2024).

studies.label: Narrative review of LLM homogenization of language, perspective, and reasoning

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing; the paper reviews published work and collects no data.
assignment.quote: We synthesize evidence across linguistics, psychology, cognitive science, and computer science to show how LLMs reflect and reinforce dominant styles while marginalizing alternative voices and reasoning strategies.

participants.who: No participants; review of published studies.

synthesis.inclusion: Not stated. Narrative review with no described search strategy or inclusion criteria; 136 numbered references (pp. 21-38). The creativity evidence it cites: refs. 124 (Anderson, Shah, and Kreminski 2024) and 125 (Doshi and Hauser 2024) on LLM-assisted ideation and semantic similarity across participants; ref. 126 (Dang et al. 2023) on deferring to model suggestions; ref. 127 (Qin et al. 2025) on timing of LLM use in ideation; ref. 128 (Kosmyna et al. 2025) on neural coupling in LLM-assisted essay writing.

company_involvement.description: Funding acknowledged from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (A9550-23-1-046); no company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: Narrative review with no human participants, no new data, and no pooled estimates (pp. 2-17). It belongs in the synthesis reference list. Its creativity claims rest on refs. 124 and 125 (p. 15), which the screening should cover as separate papers.

one_line_finding: Narrative review arguing that LLMs homogenize language, perspective, and reasoning; on creativity it cites experiments in which ChatGPT-assisted participants produced more and more elaborated ideas that were more semantically similar across participants (p. 15, refs. 124-125), with no new numbers.
open_questions: The candidate record lists the Trends in Cognitive Sciences DOI 10.1016/j.tics.2026.01.003; the file on hand is arXiv v2 (5 Jan 2026). The published version may differ in text or references.
notes: Quote supporting the creativity summary (p. 15, Reasoning Diversity): "participants who received assistance from LLMs (i.e., ChatGPT) generated a greater number of more detailed and elaborated ideas ... However, their outputs were also judged to be more semantically similar across participants [124, 125]." Figure 1 (p. 6) is a conceptual diagram with no data. The review is not systematic, so k_studies and n_effect_sizes are null.
